newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Omens of change grip HK theatre-goers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Omens of change grip HK theatre-goers.

text.p: A nightmare transformation, visions of new life and a "goodbye to all that" burst of nostalgic patriotism dominate the stage menu for Hong Kong theatre audiences in a time of fateful transition.
Dramas that concentrate on omens of change are enthralling people in this rich Asian territory, once dubbed a cultural desert but now a magnet for regional and world artists.
The fare reflects concerns at a crossroads of history, with Hong Kong reverting to China at midnight on Monday, June 30.
"Usually, art reacts slowly and late to political change, but this time we have had the unique opportunity to plan," says one producer who asked not to be identified.

Significantly, two theatres have offered separate stage versions of Franz Kafka's disturbing novel "Metamorphosis" about a salesman who turns into an insect overnight and fails to deal with the transformation.

This parable of "the unreal, the imagined, the barely conceived", already staged before in Hong Kong, struck a chord with theatre-goers ahead of Hong Kong's return to China, motherland for this 98 percent Chinese-populated land.

Director Kwong Wai-lip said the play was popular locally because Kafka's story mirrors the "Hong Kong situation", with parallels between Gregor's predicament, in suddenly becoming a changed being, and the territory's uncertain political future as a special region of China. Another director, Sean Curran, saw the play, produced here in Cantonese and English, as apolitical and a study in alienation.
BEIJING PROMISES, BUT FEARS REMAIN
Beijing has assured the British colony that its free-wheeling capitalist way of life will remain unchanged as an autonomous region of China, but many fear gradual repression of civil liberties.

Ballet productions depict scenes of revolutionary fervour -- one such being the world premiere of "The Last Emperor" on the extraordinary life of the last Manchu ruler, a "son of heaven" whom the communists turned into a gardener.

Britain is represented by an export-version of London's great summer festival of classical music, the "Last Night of the Proms," when audiences traditionally sing national favourites in an orgy of patriotic fervour.
The sun has long set on the British empire, which once covered a quarter of the globe, but here the Britons are getting round to a final salute.
Mainly Western expatriate audiences on June 27-29 will have a chance to bellow out "Rule Britannia" and wave their Union Jack flags, soon to be replaced by China's five-starred red flag.
A MIDNIGHT TRANSFORMATION - WHAT NEXT?

"When the clock strikes midnight on June 30, Hong Kong, like Cinderella, will be transformed," says a programme leaflet at City Hall, a leading stage venue, looking at the transition in fairy-tale terms.
"Will the magic be gone and her glamour lost or will she be able to retain her beauty and live happily ever after with Prince Charming?"

It adds that Hong Kong people view the return to China with mixed feelings. "They welcome the end of colonialism at the same time as dreading the possible loss of their way of life. Drastic changes always bring anxiety..."
There are fringe-theatre shows, with come-on titles like "Expose Yourself Tonight" but Hong Kong is a matter-of-fact place devoted to wealth accumulation and wary of "subverting" motherland China.

So don't expect biting satire or too many joke routines about President Jiang Zemin, who has afforded his future subjects just one light-hearted moment -- when he combed his hair in front of the King of Spain and photographers.
For middlebrow tastes, the big post-handover theatre production is "The Sound of Music", starring American singer Marie Osmond.
This decades-old show may reveal the cultural time-warp that Hong Kong is still struggling to escape.
But in a city built by refugees from mainland turmoil, audiences may see parallels in the tuneful saga of the Von Trapp family singers of Austria escaping the clutches of the Nazi Third Reich.
